description: Swiss Chard is a leafy green vegetable in the Beet family. The thick stems come in a variety of colors including white, pink, red, yellow, orange, and pale green. It has large, crinkly leaves with distinctive veins. The leaves and stems are edible and high in nutrients. Swiss chard can be eaten raw or sautéed, baked, or steamed.
sowing_method: Direct seed indoors or outdoors. Transplant seedlings after hardening off.

The part eaten is not the root, but the midrib of the leaf which is

prepared much the same as asparagus. The flavor is distinct from that

of the ordinary beet root. Give the same culture as required for beets.

The soil should be richer. In the fall cover with straw. This will aid

an early growth and help blanch the stems. This is a very valuable

plant and should be cultivated more extensively.

growing_information.text:
One of the best of the pot-herbs, though not
so generally known, is the chard or leaf-beet,
which usually requires the whole season to
mature, although it will give a succession of
leaves from early summer until fall. The leaf-blades
and midribs of the chard are very broad,
and are usually white or slightly tinted, instead
of green. Gardeners often blanch them
further by tying the leaves together while
growing. The seeds are sown in the spring as
thickly as the ordinary beet is sown, and the
plants are thinned until they stand six to twelve
inches apart in the row.

Swiss chard, also known as leaf-beet, is a valuable pot-herb that requires the whole growing season to mature but provides a succession of leaves from early summer until fall. The edible parts are the broad leaf-blades and midribs, which are typically white or slightly tinted rather than green. To cultivate Swiss chard, sow seeds in the spring as densely as you would for beets, then thin the plants to stand six to twelve inches apart in rows. The soil should be richer than that required for beets. For early growth and to help blanch the stems, cover the plants with straw in the fall. Additionally, gardeners often further blanch the leaves by tying them together while they are growing. Swiss chard is distinct from beetroot in flavor and should be prepared similarly to asparagus.
